newsitem.title: USA: Internet begins to demonstrate its value to business.
newsitem.headline: Internet begins to demonstrate its value to business.

text.p: After years of hype about the Internet's business potential, computer industry executives say it is only now beginning to demonstrate its value as a channel for sales and customer service.
The amount of business done across the Net is expected to reach $2 billion this year, double the amount seen in 1996, according to executives attending the Internet Commerce Expo here this week.

"That's not much when you realize it's a day's worth of volume for Visa and MasterCard," said Irving Wladawsky-Berger, the general manager of International Business Machines Corp.'s Internet Division.
Optimists believe Web-based business dealings could reach the $1 trillion mark by the year 2010 as more companies and their customers gain confidence about the security of online transactions.

To help start the ball rolling, IBM on Wednesday unveiled an updated version of its Net.Commerce merchant software, calling the new product the first of its kind to conform to the Secure Electronic Transaction, or SET, protocol, which is designed to make credit card numbers unreadable to outsiders on the Web.

"It's not just the technology, it's really an issue of trust," said a computer security expert. "A change of behavior, a change of culture within the business which needs to take place. That doesn't happen overnight."
To the timid, the Internet has long resembled a Wild West town full of danger for the innocent greenhorn. But for tough corporate executives, the global network of computers holds great promise.
Wells Fargo and Co., which claims to have the biggest Internet banking operation, says its Web site picks up 20,000 new online customers every two weeks.
In addition to incremental revenues, companies that have aggressively pushed the Internet as a channel for doing business report tremendous savings and return on on investment (ROI).

"The ROI numbers are staggering," said F. Selby Wellman, senior vice president of computer network equipment maker Cisco Systems Inc., which has trimmed $250 million in costs and added tens of thousands of new customers through the Internet.
"You're looking at some of these very basic applications that are producing break-evens in three to five months of implementation," he said.

The biggest obstacle so far has been a double-edged security issue. Not only are consumers reluctant to release credit card data on the Internet, but businesses have been slow to open up internal computer systems to integration with the Web.
"For very large companies, changing their infrastructures to electronic commerce is painful," said Mike Zisman, executive vice president of strategy for IBM's Lotus Development Corp. unit.

"The banks learned a lesson 20 years ago that many of us have still not learned. The lesson they learned from automatic teller machines is that you really can get customers, make them into employees and charge them for the privilege.
"The big question in the age of re-engineering, is 'How do I transfer the cost to someone else -- whoever?'" he added.
